problem: Existing navigation benchmarks and photo-realistic simulators (Gibson V1, Habitat, MINOS) use static scanned meshes, so objects cannot be moved. Their metrics (success, SPL, collision-free paths) count any contact as failure. As a result, Interactive Navigation, where pushing objects or opening doors is allowed and even needed, cannot be studied. Earlier work on it, such as NAMO planning, assumed full geometric knowledge and 2D push/pull.
motivation: Robots in cluttered homes and offices must physically interact with objects to reach goals, but doing this with real robots is expensive and risky. Physics simulation lets this be studied safely at scale, but it needs photo-realistic, interactable scenes and a metric that captures the trade-off between a short path and the effort spent disturbing the environment. Gibson V1's image-based rendering is also too slow (25-40 fps) for sample-hungry model-free RL and cannot render dynamic scenes.
key_idea: Turn Gibson's static 3D scans into physics-interactable scenes, using a fast mesh renderer and CAD models aligned in place of scanned objects, and score agents with an Interactive Navigation Score (INS) that mixes SPL-style path efficiency with a mass/force-based effort efficiency.
insight: How an agent trades path length against disturbing the scene can be tuned directly by the interaction penalty coefficient k_int in the RL reward. k_int=1 gives the highest Effort Efficiency but loses much Path Efficiency and sometimes fails outright. k_int=0.1 keeps almost the same Path Efficiency as k_int=0 while avoiding unnecessary interactions; SAC with k_int=0.1 is the best agent for every α except α=0 (Figs. 5-6). Agents learn object-class-specific behaviour (e.g., avoid sofas, push baskets) from semantic masks and embodiment: Fetch pushes more than TurtleBot. Generalization to unseen scenes is not significantly worse (one-sample t-test on INS_0.5, p=0.171), which the authors attribute to the ground-truth shortest-path waypoints in the observation.
method: Mesh renderer: replaces Gibson V1 image-based rendering with PyOpenGL/pybind11 mesh rendering. It supports dynamic scenes, reaches up to 1000 fps at 256×256, and transfers rendered images directly to GPU tensors, avoiding device-host copies.

Interactive asset pipeline: a Minkowski semantic segmentation network plus connected-component labeling produce object proposals, which in-house annotators correct (>4,000 proposals). AMT workers then pick the most similar ShapeNet CAD model and mark ≥6 keypoint correspondences in a modified Scan2CAD tool. Alignment solves a 7-DoF fit: scale 3, position 3, yaw 1.

Mesh replacement and re-texturing: scan vertices near or inside the CAD model are removed and holes filled by RANSAC plane fitting. Original texture is transferred to the CAD model, and physics settling removes floor/wall interpenetration. Density and friction are shared defaults; doors become URDF-articulated with a revolute hinge. Result: 106 scenes with 1984 interactable objects in 5 categories (chairs, desks, doors, sofas, tables).

Agents and sensing: 10 embodiments (MuJoCo humanoid/ant, Freight, JackRabbot v1/v2, Husky, TurtleBot v2, Minitaur, Fetch, Quadrotor). Observations can include RGB, depth, surface normals, semantic segmentation, pose/velocity/collisions, the goal, and the 10 next ground-truth shortest-path waypoints (0.2 m apart). Joint position/velocity control is available.

Benchmark task: point-goal navigation between random start/goal ≥1 m apart on the same floor. Ten extra scanned clutter objects (baskets, shoes, pots, toys) are placed randomly with real masses. Success means distance < robot body width within 1,000 steps (100 s).

Interactive Navigation Score: INS_α = α·P_eff + (1−α)·E_eff. P_eff = 1_suc·L*/l_0 is SPL, with L* computed without movable objects. E_eff = 0.5·(m_0 l_0 / Σ m_i l_i + T·G / (T·G + Σ F_t)) captures displaced mass (kinematic effort) and applied force (dynamic effort).

RL baselines: PPO, DDPG and SAC (from tf-agents) on TurtleBot v2 and Fetch. Inputs are goal, velocities, 10 waypoints, and 68×68 depth plus semantic mask; actions are wheel joint velocities. Reward R = R_suc (+10) + R_pot (geodesic distance decrease) + R_int (−k_int·1_int), with k_int ∈ {0, 0.1, 1}. Agents are trained on 8 scenes and tested on 2 unseen scenes, 3 seeds each.

setting.backbone: Model-free RL policies (PPO / DDPG / SAC from tf-agents) trained from scratch; network architecture not specified
setting.training_data: RL interaction in 8 randomly selected Interactive Gibson scenes with randomized clutter objects, start and goal (no external data)
setting.observation: 68×68 depth + semantic segmentation mask, goal location, linear/angular velocity, and next 10 ground-truth shortest-path waypoints (all in agent's local frame)
setting.simulator: Interactive Gibson Environment (iGibson 0.5; Bullet physics + mesh renderer)
setting.privileged: goal position in local frame, 10 next waypoints of pre-computed ground-truth shortest path (indirect map access), ground-truth semantic segmentation from simulator

numbers_note: The paper reports no numeric results tables. Baseline results (INS_α vs α for TurtleBot; Path vs Effort Efficiency for Fetch) appear only in plots (Figs. 5 and 6), and Fetch INS curves are deferred to the project page. The only printed number is the seen-vs-unseen t-test p-value of 0.171 on INS_0.5. This is a new benchmark (Interactive Gibson Benchmark / iGibson 0.5 Interactive Navigation), not one of the canonical ones.
results: SAC gives the best INS across nearly all α. SAC with k_int=0.1 performs best except at α=0, where agents with k_int=1 (minimal interaction) win. Heavy interaction penalty (k_int=1) yields the highest Effort Efficiency but greatly lowers Path Efficiency (SPL) and sometimes blocks the agent completely. k_int=0.1 matches the Path Efficiency of k_int=0 while improving Effort Efficiency. Seen and unseen scenes do not differ significantly (p=0.171 on INS_0.5); all findings come from figures, with no numeric tables.
limitations: Object physics use a common density and friction rather than real per-object values. Only 5 annotated categories plus 10 random clutter objects are interactable, and CAD-scan misalignment causes some texture distortion.

Baselines depend on privileged ground-truth shortest-path waypoints and simulator semantic masks, and are tested on only 2 unseen scenes. The authors credit the waypoints for good generalization, so the benchmark results say little about exploration or mapping.
Results are given only as plots (3 seeds, 2 robots), with no numeric tables and no non-RL (e.g., NAMO planning) baselines.
